newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader said considering extending truce.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader said considering extending truce.

text.p: The head of a European security mission mediating in the armed rebellion in southern Albania said on Saturday the country's leader was still considering extending a 48-hour ceasefire due to expire early on Sunday.

Former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky, leading the mission of the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said he had urged President Sali Berisha to extend the truce, due to expire at 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Sunday, for a further 48 hours.

Vranitzky told a news conference after a second round of talks with Berisha: "He was very open to the idea, and will give it very serious thought, and he could even imagine that it (the extension) could be longer than 48 hours."

As he was meeting Berisha and opposition leaders in Tirana, rebels in the south seized the government stronghold of Gjirokaster, putting newly arrived troops to flight and seizing thousands of weapons.

The former Austrian leader said Berisha was discussing with opposition leaders their demand for a caretaker government to run the country until new elections. Rebels who have seized major towns in the south have issued similar demands.
Vranitzky said Berisha could be more flexible on a proposal to hold elections within 45 days. The opposition objects to the time frame because of a state of emergency in force since last weekend.
"It's fair to say there might be a chance for a flexible approach as to when these (elections) might take place," Vranitzky said.
The president, backed by the opposition parties, announced the ceasefire on Friday after two days of clashes between troops and the rebels.
The rebellion was sparked by popular anger over fraudulent pyramid savings schemes in which hundreds of thousands lost money and has mushroomed into an anti-government uprising in the south.
The rebels are calling for Berisha to step down, new elections and compensation for those who lost money.

Vranitzky said earlier on Saturday that no progress could be made on measures to provide international financial aid to Albania and extend cooperation with European institutions such as the European Union until the violence was ended for good.

The OSCE mission was the latest in a series of Western initiatives to end the crisis in Albania, Europe's poorest country. Vranitzky's mission appeared in trouble earlier this week when he acknowledged that Albanian officials had told him he was not welcome in the Balkan country.
His visit to Tirana followed that of Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, representing the European Union presidency, who urged Berisha to refrain from violence.
